triage.name: Ischemic Stroke
triage.reason: Acute focal neurologic deficit with time-critical workup and thrombolysis decisions; a core emergency and neurology case.

presentation: older format without SNOMED terms
exam: older format without SNOMED terms

demographics: Risk rises sharply with age; most strokes occur in adults over 60
More common in Black and Hispanic adults than in White adults in the US
Men have a higher age-adjusted incidence than women, but women have more strokes overall because they live longer
Stroke is a leading cause of long-term disability in adults

risk_factors.text: Prior stroke or transient ischemic attack
Migraine with aura in younger women

comorbidities: Coronary artery disease or heart failure
family_history: Stroke or transient ischemic attack in a first-degree relative
Premature coronary artery disease in the family

chief_complaints.text: All of a sudden my right arm and leg went weak
My face feels droopy on one side
My words are coming out slurred and wrong
I suddenly can't see out of one eye
I feel dizzy and can't keep my balance

hpi.onset: Sudden, maximal or near-maximal within seconds to minutes; patients often can name the exact moment it started
hpi.duration: Symptoms are still present at presentation; deficits that fully clear within minutes to an hour suggest a transient ischemic attack
hpi.progression: Deficit is worst at onset and then stable or slowly improving; stepwise worsening or fluctuation over hours is less typical
hpi.location: Depends on the artery involved: one side of the face, arm and leg (middle cerebral), one side of the body with leg worse than arm (anterior cerebral), or face/arm/leg with crossed findings and vertigo or diplopia (posterior circulation)
hpi.quality: Loss of strength, sensation or vision rather than pain; numbness is described as 'dead' or 'asleep'
hpi.severity: Often severe and frightening; weakness can be complete or partial, and speech may be unintelligible
hpi.timing: Abrupt onset at any time of day; a substantial minority occur during sleep and are noticed on waking

associated_symptoms.text: Weakness or clumsiness of one arm and leg
Numbness or loss of feeling on one side
Trouble finding words or understanding what others say
Loss of vision in one eye or to one side
Confusion or trouble following a conversation

pertinent_negatives: Thunderclap headache that was worst at the very first second
Vomiting at onset followed by rapid loss of consciousness
Fever or rash before the weakness
Symptoms that spread gradually over hours or days
Symptoms that come and go repeatedly over weeks
Sudden painless loss of vision that clears like a curtain lifting (suggests amaurosis fugax rather than completed stroke)

argues_against: Fluctuating weakness that worsens with fatigue (suggests neuromuscular junction or demyelinating disease)

positives.text: Loss of vision in one eye
Loss of vision to one side

argues_against: Painful red eye with visual loss (suggests acute glaucoma or uveitis)
Chest pain with radiation to the arm and jaw (suggests acute coronary syndrome)
Fever with rash and headache (suggests infection or vasculitis)
Vomiting before the weakness started (suggests hemorrhage or metabolic cause)

positives.text: Weakness of one arm and leg

argues_against: Painful, swollen joint (suggests arthritis or infection)

atypical.how_it_differs: May present with confusion, falls or sudden inability to walk rather than clear one-sided weakness; deficits can be mistaken for delirium.
Rare; often presents with seizures, altered mental status or isolated hemiparesis, and is frequently attributed to other causes first.
missing_classic_features: Sudden focal deficit recognized by the family

atypical.how_it_differs: Can occur in the postpartum period from cerebral venous thrombosis or from eclampsia; headache and seizures are more prominent.
Sensory deficits may be blunted by pre-existing neuropathy, so weakness or speech change is noticed more than numbness.
missing_classic_features: New numbness as a clear symptom

general.mild: Alert, awake, speaking in full sentences; mild one-sided weakness or facial droop may be the only obvious sign
general.moderate: Awake but visibly impaired; may have slurred speech, drift of one arm, or difficulty walking; able to follow simple commands
general.severe: Drowsy or inattentive; dense one-sided weakness, marked speech difficulty, may not protect the airway
general.critical: Stuporous or unresponsive; dense hemiplegia, gaze deviation, may have impaired airway protection and breathing

findings.maneuver: Ask the patient to smile or show their teeth
findings.finding: One side of the face droops; the nasolabial fold is flattened on the affected side

findings.maneuver: Have the patient hold both arms out in front with eyes closed for 10 seconds
findings.finding: One arm drifts downward or cannot be held up

findings.maneuver: Have the patient lift each leg off the bed against gravity, then apply resistance
findings.finding: Weakness of one leg, often with the arm on the same side

findings.maneuver: Ask the patient to repeat a simple phrase such as 'the sky is blue'
findings.finding: Slurred or garbled speech with preserved language comprehension

findings.maneuver: Ask the patient to name common objects and follow a two-step command
findings.finding: Trouble finding words, paraphasic errors, or poor comprehension

findings.maneuver: Test light touch and pinprick on both sides of the face, arms and legs
findings.finding: Reduced or absent sensation on one side of the body

findings.maneuver: Confrontation visual field testing in all four quadrants
findings.finding: Loss of one side of the visual field in both eyes (homonymous hemianopia) or loss of vision in one eye

findings.maneuver: Observe the direction of the eyes at rest and with voluntary gaze
findings.finding: Both eyes deviate toward the side of the brain lesion
Clumsy, overshooting movements on one side, suggesting cerebellar or posterior circulation involvement

findings.maneuver: Inspect for nystagmus with the patient following your finger to the left and right
findings.finding: Repetitive involuntary eye movements, often with vertigo and imbalance

findings.maneuver: Observe the patient swallowing a small sip of water or ask about coughing with liquids
findings.finding: Coughing, choking or wet voice after swallowing

findings.maneuver: Ask the patient to sit up and, if safe, stand and take a few steps with assistance
findings.finding: Unsteady, wide-based or veering gait; may be unable to walk

findings.maneuver: Gently flex the neck and check for resistance
findings.finding: No neck stiffness or meningismus

findings.maneuver: Measure temperature and inspect for rash
findings.finding: No fever and no rash

findings.maneuver: Palpate the radial pulse and auscultate the heart
findings.finding: Irregularly irregular rhythm suggesting atrial fibrillation
Bruit over one or both carotids suggesting stenosis

findings.maneuver: Ask about the character and timing of any headache
findings.finding: No thunderclap headache that was worst at the very first second

findings.maneuver: Ask about witnessed seizure activity or loss of consciousness at onset
findings.finding: No seizure and no loss of consciousness at onset

labs.caveat: Must be checked before thrombolysis; hypoglycemia is a common stroke mimic and hyperglycemia worsens outcome.
An elevated INR from warfarin is a contraindication to IV thrombolysis; it also raises suspicion for hemorrhagic stroke.
Prolonged by heparin or a coagulopathy; relevant before thrombolysis.
Severe anemia can worsen cerebral ischemia and may point to a bleeding source.
A marked leukocytosis or fever should raise concern for infection or endocarditis rather than stroke alone.
Needed before contrast CT angiography and to gauge renal reserve.
Mild elevation is common from demand ischemia or concurrent cardiac ischemia; a rising pattern suggests acute coronary syndrome as the embolic source.
Identifies undiagnosed or poorly controlled diabetes as a modifiable risk factor.
Guides high-intensity statin therapy for secondary prevention.
Negative. Required in anyone who could be pregnant before CT angiography or thrombolysis.

findings.finding: Irregularly irregular rhythm without discrete P waves, consistent with atrial fibrillation
Sinus rhythm
ST-segment elevation or depression suggesting concurrent acute coronary syndrome
Left ventricular hypertrophy from chronic hypertension
Prolonged QT interval that would limit use of certain antiarrhythmics

imaging.preferred_when: First-line in every suspected acute stroke to exclude hemorrhage

findings.text: No acute hemorrhage
Early ischemic changes such as loss of gray-white differentiation, insular ribbon sign, or sulcal effacement
Hyperdense middle cerebral artery sign
Established hypodense infarct in the affected vascular territory
Intracerebral hemorrhage, which would exclude ischemic stroke

imaging.study: CT angiography of the head and neck
imaging.preferred_when: Suspected large-vessel occlusion being considered for thrombectomy

findings.text: Abrupt cutoff or filling defect in an intracranial artery (for example the M1 segment of the middle cerebral artery)
Carotid or vertebral artery stenosis or occlusion
No large-vessel occlusion

imaging.preferred_when: Extended time window or unclear onset, to identify salvageable tissue

findings.text: Mismatch between the ischemic core and the larger area of hypoperfused but potentially salvageable tissue
Large established core with little salvageable tissue

imaging.study: MRI of the brain with diffusion-weighted imaging
imaging.preferred_when: Small or posterior circulation strokes, or when CT is nondiagnostic

findings.text: Restricted diffusion with bright signal on diffusion-weighted imaging and low signal on the apparent diffusion coefficient map in a vascular territory
Corresponding fluid-attenuated inversion recovery changes that are less extensive than the diffusion abnormality (diffusion-FLAIR mismatch) in early stroke
Multiple small embolic infarcts in more than one territory, suggesting a cardioembolic source

imaging.preferred_when: Screening for carotid stenosis when CT angiography is not available or is contraindicated

findings.text: Increased peak systolic velocity with plaque at the carotid bifurcation indicating stenosis
No hemodynamically significant stenosis
Left atrial enlargement or spontaneous echo contrast
Left ventricular thrombus or wall-motion abnormality from prior infarction
Valvular vegetation suggesting endocarditis
Patent foramen ovale on agitated saline study

imaging.preferred_when: Cryptogenic stroke or when a cardiac source is strongly suspected but transthoracic study is unrevealing

findings.text: Left atrial appendage thrombus
Aortic arch atheroma
Patent foramen ovale or atrial septal defect
Usually normal; may show cardiomegaly or pulmonary edema

initial.why: Excludes hemorrhage and is required before any thrombolytic; fastest first study in acute stroke
Hypoglycemia is a common and immediately reversible stroke mimic
Baseline platelets and hemoglobin before thrombolysis and to look for infection
PT/INR and aPTT are needed before thrombolysis
Electrolytes, renal function and glucose before contrast and thrombolysis
Detects atrial fibrillation and concurrent acute coronary syndrome
Looks for concurrent cardiac ischemia as a stroke cause or complication
Rules out pregnancy before CT angiography and thrombolysis
initial.only_if: patient is a woman of childbearing potential

initial.test: CT angiography of the head and neck
initial.why: Identifies large-vessel occlusion for possible thrombectomy
initial.only_if: large-vessel occlusion is suspected or the patient is a thrombectomy candidate

initial.why: Identifies salvageable tissue in an extended or unclear time window
initial.only_if: onset time is unknown or beyond the standard thrombolysis window

confirmatory.test: MRI of the brain with diffusion-weighted imaging
confirmatory.why: Most sensitive for acute infarction, especially small or posterior circulation strokes and when CT is nondiagnostic

supporting.why: Identifies undiagnosed or poorly controlled diabetes
Guides statin therapy for secondary prevention
Searches for a cardioembolic source such as atrial thrombus or valvular disease

supporting.only_if: stroke is cryptogenic or a cardiac source is strongly suspected

supporting.why: Assesses carotid stenosis when CT angiography is unavailable or contraindicated

not_indicated.why: Not routine; reserved for suspected subarachnoid hemorrhage with a negative CT or for suspected central nervous system infection
No role in diagnosing ischemic stroke
Not indicated unless abdominal pain suggests pancreatitis
Not part of the acute stroke evaluation

decision_points: Noncontrast head CT must be done and hemorrhage excluded before giving a thrombolytic
Check glucose immediately; treat hypoglycemia as a reversible stroke mimic
Establish the last known well time to decide thrombolysis eligibility
Pregnancy test before CT angiography or thrombolysis in anyone who could be pregnant
Suspected large-vessel occlusion should prompt CT angiography and thrombectomy evaluation

differential.name: Hemorrhagic stroke
differential.why_considered: Presents with the same sudden focal neurologic deficit as ischemic stroke and is the most important thing to exclude before giving a thrombolytic.
differential.trigger: Thunderclap headache, vomiting at onset, rapid decline in consciousness, or a head CT showing hyperdense blood

history: Sudden severe headache that was worst at the very first second
Vomiting at onset
Rapid loss of consciousness or early drowsiness
Known uncontrolled hypertension or anticoagulant use
exam: Deteriorating level of consciousness out of proportion to the focal deficit
labs: Elevated INR from warfarin or prolonged aPTT from heparin
imaging: Hyperdense blood in the brain parenchyma, ventricles or subarachnoid space on noncontrast CT
No restricted diffusion in a vascular territory on MRI

differential.name: Hypoglycemia
differential.why_considered: A common, immediately reversible stroke mimic that can cause focal weakness, aphasia or altered mental status.
differential.trigger: Glucose below 60 mg/dL in a patient with a sudden focal deficit

history: Diabetes treated with insulin or a sulfonylurea
Missed meal, excess insulin or recent alcohol use
Prior episodes that resolved with sugar
exam: Deficit resolves after glucose is given
labs: Low serum glucose that corrects the symptoms
imaging: No acute infarct on CT or MRI

differential.name: Seizure with postictal Todd paralysis
differential.why_considered: A focal seizure can leave one-sided weakness that looks like a stroke, especially in the first hours.
differential.trigger: Witnessed seizure activity or loss of consciousness at onset followed by focal weakness

history: Witnessed tonic-clonic or focal motor activity before the weakness
Loss of consciousness at onset
Tongue biting or incontinence during the event
Known epilepsy or prior similar episodes
exam: Weakness improves over minutes to hours
No gaze deviation or clear vascular territory pattern
labs: Elevated creatine kinase or lactate after a generalized seizure
imaging: No acute infarct on CT or MRI
May show an old structural lesion or epileptogenic focus

differential.name: Complex migraine with aura
differential.why_considered: Can cause transient one-sided weakness, numbness, speech difficulty or visual loss that mimics a stroke.

history: Gradual spread of symptoms over minutes rather than sudden onset
Positive phenomena such as flashing lights, zigzag lines or tingling that marches
Prior similar episodes, often with headache
Younger patient without vascular risk factors
exam: Normal strength and sensation between episodes

differential.name: Bell palsy
differential.why_considered: Sudden one-sided facial droop is often mistaken for a stroke.

history: Weakness limited to the face, with no arm or leg involvement
Often preceded by ear pain or a viral illness
exam: Inability to close the eye and forehead sparing is absent (whole side of face involved, including the forehead)
No arm or leg weakness, no aphasia

differential.name: Peripheral vertigo (vestibular neuritis or labyrinthitis)
differential.why_considered: Sudden dizziness, imbalance and nystagmus can resemble a posterior circulation stroke.

history: Gradual onset of spinning vertigo over hours
No focal weakness, numbness or speech difficulty
Recent viral illness
exam: Unidirectional horizontal nystagmus that suppresses with fixation
Normal gait or only mild unsteadiness
imaging: No acute infarct on MRI, especially in the cerebellum or brainstem

differential.name: Todd paralysis after a metabolic disturbance (hyperglycemia or hyponatremia)
differential.why_considered: Severe metabolic derangements can cause focal deficits or altered mental status that mimic stroke.

history: Known diabetes with very high glucose, or diuretic use with confusion
Symptoms fluctuate or are diffuse rather than a clear vascular pattern
exam: Altered mental status out of proportion to focal findings
Deficit improves as the metabolic abnormality is corrected
labs: Markedly elevated glucose or low sodium
imaging: No acute infarct on CT or MRI

severity.mild: Small infarct with mild deficit (for example mild arm weakness or facial droop), patient alert and able to walk and swallow safely; NIHSS typically low
severity.moderate: Clear focal deficit such as dense one-sided weakness, aphasia or visual field cut; patient awake but needs help with some activities; may be a candidate for thrombolysis or thrombectomy
severity.severe: Large territory infarct with dense hemiplegia, marked aphasia or neglect, drowsiness, and risk of airway compromise or malignant edema
severity.critical: Large hemispheric or brainstem infarct with impaired consciousness, airway compromise, malignant cerebral edema, or herniation; may require ICU care and decompressive surgery

red_flags.finding: Sudden severe headache that was worst at the very first second
red_flags.meaning: Suggests subarachnoid or intracerebral hemorrhage rather than ischemic stroke

red_flags.finding: Vomiting at onset followed by rapid loss of consciousness
red_flags.meaning: Suggests hemorrhage or a large infarct with raised intracranial pressure
Hypoglycemia is a reversible stroke mimic; treat immediately

red_flags.finding: Deteriorating level of consciousness after admission
red_flags.meaning: Suggests malignant cerebral edema, hemorrhagic transformation or another complication

red_flags.finding: New severe headache, vomiting or sudden decline after thrombolysis
Coughing or choking with liquids, or a wet voice
red_flags.meaning: Dysphagia with high aspiration risk; keep the patient NPO until swallowing is assessed

red_flags.finding: Irregularly irregular pulse with a focal deficit
red_flags.meaning: Suggests atrial fibrillation as the embolic source and guides anticoagulation planning

complications.name: Hemorrhagic transformation of the infarct
clues: Sudden headache, vomiting or decline in consciousness
Follow-up CT showing blood within the infarct

complications.name: Malignant cerebral edema
clues: Progressive drowsiness over the first 24–72 hours
Headache, vomiting, pupillary change or herniation signs

complications.name: Aspiration pneumonia
clues: Fever, hypoxemia or new infiltrate on chest x-ray

complications.name: Deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism
Urinary tract infection
clues: Fever, cloudy urine or new confusion

complications.name: Post-stroke depression
clues: Persistent low mood, loss of interest or poor participation in rehabilitation weeks after the stroke

complications.name: Vascular dementia or cognitive impairment
clues: Stepwise decline in memory and thinking
Multiple infarcts or strategic infarct location on imaging

complications.name: Recurrent stroke
clues: Uncontrolled hypertension, atrial fibrillation or carotid stenosis
New focal deficit during the same admission or in follow-up

special_populations.differences: May present with confusion, falls or sudden inability to walk rather than clear one-sided weakness; deficits can be mistaken for delirium. Higher risk of complications and worse outcomes.
Rare; often presents with seizures, altered mental status or isolated hemiparesis. Sickle cell disease, congenital heart disease and vasculopathy are important causes.

Can occur in pregnancy or the postpartum period from cerebral venous thrombosis, eclampsia or cardioembolic sources. Headache and seizures are more prominent, and imaging and treatment must account for the fetus.
Pre-existing neuropathy can blunt sensory symptoms, so weakness or speech change is noticed more than numbness. Hyperglycemia at presentation worsens outcome.
Contrast CT angiography and perfusion carry a higher risk of contrast-induced nephropathy; renal function should be checked and alternative imaging considered when possible.

key_questions.question: When was the patient last known to be well, and when exactly did the symptoms start?
key_questions.looking_for: A precise last known well time; this determines eligibility for IV thrombolysis and thrombectomy

key_questions.question: Did the symptoms start suddenly, and were they worst right at the beginning?
key_questions.looking_for: Abrupt onset reaching maximal deficit within seconds to minutes, the hallmark of a vascular event

key_questions.question: What exactly is affected — face, arm, leg, speech, vision, balance? Is it one side of the body?
key_questions.looking_for: A focal deficit in a vascular territory, such as face, arm and leg on one side with or without aphasia

key_questions.question: Has the weakness or speech problem been getting better, worse, or staying the same?
key_questions.looking_for: Stable or slowly improving deficit; fluctuation or stepwise worsening is less typical

key_questions.question: Did you have any sudden severe headache, vomiting, or loss of consciousness at the start?
key_questions.looking_for: Thunderclap headache, vomiting at onset or early loss of consciousness, which point toward hemorrhage

key_questions.question: Did anyone see you have a seizure or pass out before the weakness started?
key_questions.looking_for: Witnessed seizure activity or loss of consciousness, suggesting postictal Todd paralysis rather than stroke

key_questions.question: Do you have high blood pressure, diabetes, high cholesterol, atrial fibrillation, or have you had a stroke or TIA before?
key_questions.looking_for: Vascular risk factors that make an ischemic stroke likely and guide secondary prevention

key_questions.question: Do you take any blood thinners, such as warfarin, apixaban, rivaroxaban or aspirin?
key_questions.looking_for: Anticoagulant use, which affects thrombolysis eligibility and raises concern for hemorrhage

key_questions.question: Do you smoke, drink alcohol heavily, or use cocaine or amphetamines?
key_questions.looking_for: Modifiable risk factors and stimulant use, which can cause stroke in younger patients

key_questions.question: Has anyone in your family had a stroke or a heart attack at a young age?
key_questions.looking_for: A family history that raises suspicion for inherited clotting or lipid disorders

key_questions.question: Have you had any recent head trauma, fever, rash, or infection?
key_questions.looking_for: Absent; present would suggest trauma, infection or vasculitis as an alternative cause

key_questions.question: Could you be pregnant? When was your last menstrual period?
key_questions.looking_for: Pregnancy status, which is required before CT angiography or thrombolysis in anyone who could be pregnant

key_questions.question: Have you had trouble swallowing, or coughed or choked when drinking liquids?
key_questions.looking_for: Dysphagia with aspiration risk; the patient should be kept NPO until swallowing is assessed

key_questions.question: Do you have any chest pain, palpitations, or shortness of breath?
key_questions.looking_for: Atrial fibrillation or concurrent acute coronary syndrome as a stroke cause or complication

reasoning_points: Sudden onset of a focal neurologic deficit that was maximal at the start
Deficit fits a vascular territory, such as one-sided face, arm and leg weakness with or without aphasia
Vascular risk factors present, such as hypertension, atrial fibrillation, diabetes, smoking or prior stroke or TIA
Noncontrast head CT excludes hemorrhage before any thrombolytic is given
Glucose checked and hypoglycemia excluded as a reversible stroke mimic
Last known well time established to decide thrombolysis and thrombectomy eligibility
CT angiography identifies a large-vessel occlusion that may be treatable by thrombectomy
MRI with diffusion-weighted imaging confirms acute infarction when CT is nondiagnostic
Cardiac and carotid sources are sought, including atrial fibrillation on ECG and carotid stenosis on vascular imaging

easy: Older adult with hypertension and atrial fibrillation
Abrupt one-sided face, arm and leg weakness with slurred speech
Clear last known well time within the thrombolysis window
Noncontrast head CT shows no hemorrhage
medium: Posterior circulation stroke with dizziness, double vision and imbalance rather than clear hemiparesis
Small lacunar infarct with pure motor or pure sensory deficit and a normal-appearing early CT
Woman of reproductive age with migraine history and a focal deficit that must be distinguished from complex migraine
Patient on warfarin with an elevated INR, complicating thrombolysis decisions
hard: Wake-up stroke with an unknown last known well time, requiring perfusion imaging to assess salvageable tissue
Older adult presenting with confusion or a fall rather than clear one-sided weakness
Patient with a focal deficit whose glucose is low, requiring treatment of hypoglycemia before assuming stroke
Suspected large-vessel occlusion needing rapid CT angiography and thrombectomy evaluation
Young patient with stroke from carotid dissection or stimulant use and no classic vascular risk factors
